_doc: Tabbed interactive HTML report (build_html_report.py). Calibrate here: tab groups, tab order, titles, intros, components, branding, glossary. Components: kpis, chart:r7, chart:severity, chart:segments, chart:categories, apps-table, app-plans, linux-scorecard, linux-checks, linux-issues, linux-build, findings:<segment id>|all, package-groups, packages-table, binaries-table, integrations-summary, thirdparty-table, onprem-table, sdk-table, effort-summary, workpackages-table, block:optional (optional modernizations), gantt, architecture-map, dependencies-table, questions-table, projects-table, winapi-table, glossary, next-steps, pilot, waves, order-table, repo-order, projects-7r, project-graph, deployable-needs, graph-links, work-items, auth, package-actions (developer screens: migration order, per-project 7R and difficulty, dependencies, code graph, work items, sign-in and access, package actions), narrative:<name> (any file in assessment/narrative/), block:<name> (any Markdown block from build_report.py). Segment ids: linux, modernization, packages, integrations, data, security, hosting, delivery. Narrative files not placed in any tab appear in an 'Additional notes' tab.

brand.confidential_note: Confidential — prepared for {client}. Contains architecture and security findings.

tabs.title: Overview
tabs.intro: What to do first, what we recommend, how long it takes and the main risks. Each line under 'What to do first' opens the screen that has the detail.

tabs.title: Migration order
tabs.intro: Which project to move first and why. A project moves once everything it depends on has moved; projects many others depend on (high blast radius) move early and are retested with every deployable that uses them. Select a project for its 7R, difficulty and dependencies.

tabs.title: Projects & 7R
tabs.intro: Every project, class libraries and test projects included: what kind it is, how hard it is to port (APIs, class libraries and console / worker projects are easy; Web Forms and desktop UIs are hard), and its own 7R. Below, the deployable applications with effort and the full reasoning.

tabs.title: Dependencies
tabs.intro: What each deployable needs ported first, the project dependency map by wave, and how applications, data and external systems connect.

tabs.title: Code graph
tabs.intro: Explore the code itself: blast radius of a class or file, dependency paths, hubs, call flows and the generated wiki. The explorer opens in a new tab and works offline.

tabs.title: Work items
tabs.intro: Everything to change, grouped by project in migration order: what to do, why, and where in the code. Blocker and High first.

tabs.title: Sign-in & access
tabs.intro: How each application signs users and callers in, how it decides what they may do, and the recommended replacement on ASP.NET Core and AWS, with the developer steps and the questions for the client. All security findings follow.

tabs.title: Packages
tabs.intro: What to do with every NuGet package: upgrade for a security advisory, replace, remove, upgrade, get the source, check the licence, or keep. Select a tile to filter. DLLs referenced outside NuGet follow.

tabs.title: Linux readiness
tabs.intro: Can each application run on Linux, and what stops it? Readiness per application, every issue type that breaks on Linux, then every Linux readiness check that hit and how the estimate counts it.

tabs.title: .NET modernization
tabs.intro: Technologies that do not exist on modern .NET (System.Web, Web Forms, WCF, desktop UI, AppDomains, Remoting) and framework versions out of support.

tabs.title: Integrations & AWS landing
tabs.intro: External services and APIs the code calls, on-premises systems it depends on, service SDKs, identity providers, email and file transfer, and the network allow-list (outbound destinations with ports, inbound listeners) for the AWS VPC.

tabs.title: Data & database
tabs.intro: Which AWS database fits, what blocks the alternatives, and data-access code that changes.

tabs.title: Hosting & operations
tabs.intro: Scheduled and background jobs (what runs when, configured how, Windows-only schedulers), iIS, session and state, scaling, background jobs, logging and machine coupling.

tabs.title: Delivery & quality
tabs.intro: Build, CI/CD, tests, front end and parallel development.

tabs.title: Effort & timeline
tabs.intro: Coding effort in hours and person-days for the selected scenario (AI-assisted delivery, manual equivalent alongside), the code-side and database-code scenarios side by side, optional modernizations, the phased plan, the coding sprint plan from the day of codebase access, and licensing. Ranges are P10–P90 (80% confidence); likely is P50. The last section explains how the estimate was calculated, step by step.

tabs.title: Application plans
tabs.intro: The approach, shared libraries kept on .NET Standard 2.0 while others move (hybrid path), and the decision per application.

tabs.title: Risks & questions
tabs.intro: What could change the plan, and what we need the client to answer.

tabs.title: All findings
tabs.intro: Every finding with evidence. Filter by segment, severity, category or application; click a row for the details and the fix.

tabs.title: Scope & method
tabs.intro: What we looked at, how, what could not be assessed from code, and the glossary.

tabs.title: Appendices
tabs.intro: Complete lists for the delivery team.

glossary: Cannot run on Linux / modern .NET until a technology is replaced or the app is kept on Windows.
Needs code or design change before go-live.
Needs change, contained to a few places.
Clean-up or hardening; not on the critical path.
How sure we are: seen in code / pattern seen but not fully traced / depends on servers or data we could not see.
Switch the application off (duplicate or no longer used).
Keep as it is for now (for example a desktop app, or an app staying on .NET Framework).
Move as-is to AWS (lift and shift), usually onto Windows servers.
Move with moderate changes: port to .NET 10 and run on Linux in AWS, same design.
Change the design to move: for example rewrite a user interface or replace a technology.
Replace with a product (SaaS) / move a whole virtualised environment unchanged.
Effort for one person; 1 person-day = 8 hours. Ranges show low and high; 'likely' is the planning figure.
The mechanical port is done with AWS Transform for .NET, GitHub Copilot app modernization or coding agents and reviewed by engineers; testing and cut-over are not shortened much.
Keep one app on the old .NET Framework while others move; shared code is built so both can use it.
The current long-term-support version of .NET, supported until November 2028; runs on Linux.
A group of projects that can move together: everything they depend on moved in an earlier wave. Projects in a dependency cycle share a wave.
How much breaks or must be retested when a project changes: the projects and deployables that depend on it, directly or through others, plus how often other files use its code.

How hard a project is to port. Easy: APIs, class libraries, console and worker projects. Medium: service hosts, MVC UIs, or easy projects with blockers. Hard: Web Forms and desktop UIs (rewritten), Windows-bound code, very large projects.
The first deployable to move: easy, few projects before it, little depends on it. It proves the build, container, deploy and test pipeline.
